topics.title: Chapter 58 — Exploit Mitigations
topics.summary: Mitigations reduce the consequences or feasibility of exploiting certain bugs. They are defense in depth, not substitutes for memory safety. A program can contain a serious vulnerability even when it is compiled with hardening flags, uses randomized addresses, and has non-executable data pages. Treat mitigation status as a property to inspect in the actual build and deployment. A flag written in a document is not evidence that the final executable or runtime environment enforces the intended protection. [ R3 , R31 , R45 ]

topics.title: 58.1 Stack canaries
topics.summary: Stack-protector instrumentation places a check value in selected stack frames and verifies it before returning through the protected path. Some overwrites can then be detected before corrupted state is used in a normal return sequence. Coverage depends on compiler options and generated code. A canary does not prevent the original out-of-bounds write, protect every object, or guarantee detection of every corruption pattern. It is a detection barrier for a subset of consequences.

topics.title: 58.2 Non-executable memory
topics.summary: Non-executable permissions prevent instruction fetches from designated data regions. Separating executable code from writable data reduces one class of attack opportunity. The processor and operating system must support and enforce the mapping policy. Non-executable data does not prevent all control-flow misuse or data-only corruption. An attacker does not necessarily need to introduce new executable bytes to cause harm. The underlying invalid write, stale pointer, or authorization error still requires repair.

topics.title: 58.3 Address-space randomization
topics.summary: Address-space randomization varies locations of mapped regions to make useful addresses less predictable. Position-independent executables and libraries support relocation under the relevant loader model. Randomization is not confidentiality by itself. Information disclosure can reveal addresses, and entropy varies with architecture and configuration. Do not disable randomization to make an application appear more stable; investigate invalid address assumptions instead.

topics.title: 58.4 Memory permissions
topics.summary: Memory permissions restrict reading, writing, and execution at mapping granularity. A least-permission design avoids writable executable regions and removes unneeded access. Read-only mappings can protect immutable tables from accidental modification. Changing permissions is a privileged service request and may require translation invalidation. Permissions still do not distinguish two objects inside one writable page. They reinforce region-level boundaries while language and application rules govern object-level behavior.

topics.title: 58.5 Privilege separation
topics.summary: Privilege separation divides a system so that components handling untrusted input possess only the authority they need. A small privileged component can perform narrow validated operations for a less-privileged parser or worker. The communication interface becomes a security boundary and must validate message type, size, identity, and requested action. Splitting into processes without reducing authority or validating requests merely relocates the same risk. Failure recovery should also specify what happens when one component exits midway through an operation.

topics.title: Worked example — Build and inspect a hardened parser
topics.summary: The following script compiles the safe Chapter 57 parser with a representative GNU/Linux hardening configuration. It uses the installed compiler and standard library; it does not download software, change kernel settings, or disable any protection. Support for individual options depends on the toolchain. Companion listing: ch58/harden.sh Inspection should distinguish evidence from inference. A position-independent executable normally appears as ELF type DYN with executable context; a GNU_STACK program header should not request execute permission; GNU_RELRO and immediate-binding metadata provide evidence for the requested relocation protections. These observations do not prove that every mitigation is effective on every path, nor that the program has no vulnerabilities. [ R37 , R45 ] _FORTIFY_SOURCE=3 requires a supporting compiler and libc environment and useful optimization. A build failure should be reported and the supported configuration selected deliberately, not hidden by silently dropping flags while continuing to label the output hardened. Sanitizer builds serve a different testing purpose and should be documented separately.

SLIDE 1: Chapter 58 — Exploit Mitigations

LECTURE NARRATION
Mitigations reduce the consequences or feasibility of exploiting certain bugs. They are defense in depth, not substitutes for memory safety. A program can contain a serious vulnerability even when it is compiled with hardening flags, uses randomized addresses, and has non-executable data pages. Treat mitigation status as a property to inspect in the actual build and deployment. A flag written in a document is not evidence that the final executable or runtime environment enforces the intended protection. [ R3 , R31 , R45 ]

At graduate level, do not treat this as a term to memorize. Identify the contract being described, the state or representation it constrains, and the assumptions that must remain true. When this topic appears in real systems code, separate what the language guarantees from what a compiler, operating system, ABI, ISA, or particular machine happens to do. Then identify the evidence you would inspect to test the claim without overgeneralizing from a single successful run.
